docs.title: Preface
docs.text:
This guide helps Java developers familiar with Spring understand GraphQL and build GraphQL APIs with Spring GraphQL and the Netflix DGS framework. It starts with the GraphQL specification and its transport protocols, then covers GraphQL Java — the execution engine that every JVM framework builds on — and finishes with the two Spring-based frameworks, their history, and their relationship.

The examples use Java 25 and Spring Boot 4.1.2 / Spring Framework 7. Some examples are written in Kotlin (Kotlin 2.4.x). This guide is not a Spring tutorial; it assumes you can already build a Spring Boot application.

docs.title: Get the examples
docs.text:
The spring-graphql-sample repository contains the example projects. Clone it with Git:

git clone https://github.com/hantsy/spring-graphql-sample.git

Each example is a standalone Maven project with its own Maven Wrapper. See the README for the full example index and build instructions.

docs.title: Read this guide
docs.text:
Read the sections in order if you are new to GraphQL on the JVM:

  1. Introduction to GraphQL — the specification, the schema language, and the HTTP and WebSocket transports.
  2. GraphQL Java — the core concepts of the execution engine, and the integration history of GraphQL in the Java ecosystem.
  3. Netflix DGS and Spring GraphQL — the two frameworks, their integration, and how to choose.

docs.title: Contribute
docs.text: Report an issue or propose a change through a pull request in the GitHub repository.

docs.title: Netflix DGS and Spring GraphQL
docs.text:
Two Spring Boot frameworks dominate GraphQL on the JVM today, and since 2024 they are no longer competitors at the engine level: the Netflix DGS framework is built on Spring GraphQL. This section introduces both, explains the integration, and compares them so you can choose.

  • Netflix DGS (Domain Graph Service) — Netflix's GraphQL server framework for Spring Boot, open-sourced in 2021. An annotation-based programming model (@DgsComponent, @DgsQuery), schema code generation, and federation support.
  • Spring GraphQL — the Spring team's official GraphQL support, built on GraphQL Java, 1.0 in May 2022. A Spring MVC-style controller model (@QueryMapping, @SchemaMapping), GraphQlTester, and HTTP, WebSocket, and RSocket transports.

Both execute operations with GraphQL Java. Since DGS 9, DGS also uses Spring GraphQL's execution and transport infrastructure — the choice between them is a choice of programming model and extras, not of engine.

docs.title: In this section
docs.text:
1. Netflix DGS — the DGS programming model, codegen, federation, and testing.
  2. Spring GraphQL — the controller model, transports, testing, and clients.
  3. The DGS and Spring GraphQL integration — why and how the two frameworks merged their foundations.
  4. DGS or Spring GraphQL? — the differences that remain, and how to choose.

docs.title: DGS or Spring GraphQL?
docs.text: Since the integration, DGS and Spring GraphQL share the same foundation: both run on Spring Boot, both execute operations with GraphQL Java, and DGS additionally uses Spring GraphQL's execution service and transports. The differences that remain are the programming model and the tooling around it.

docs.title: Differences
docs.text:
Aspect Netflix DGS Spring GraphQL Programming model @DgsComponent classes with @DgsQuery, @DgsData, @InputArgument @Controller classes with @QueryMapping, @SchemaMapping, @Argument Schema location src/main/resources/schema/ src/main/resources/graphql/ Code generation Official Gradle/Maven plugin generates types from the schema No built-in codegen; use a third-party plugin if wanted Federation Built-in subgraph support Not built in; add a federation library Testing DgsQueryExecutor, @DgsTest GraphQlTester, @GraphQlTest, transport testers Client Typesafe client generated from the schema HttpSyncGraphQlClient, HttpGraphQlClient, WebSocketGraphQlClient Transports HTTP, SSE, WebSocket (via Spring GraphQL) HTTP, SSE, WebSocket, RSocket Stewardship Netflix Spring team Dependency management DGS platform BOM aligned to a Boot version Spring Boot starter, version managed by Boot

Both frameworks support Kotlin and coroutines, Spring Security, file uploads through MultipartFile, and DataLoader-based batching. The dgs-kotlin-co and spring-graphql-rsocket-kotlin-co examples show the two styles side by side.

docs.title: Choose
docs.text:
• Starting a new Spring Boot application — choose Spring GraphQL. It is the official Spring baseline, its versions move with Spring Boot, and its controller model matches the rest of a Spring application.
  • Running DGS today — stay on DGS and keep upgrading. Since DGS 9 you are already on Spring GraphQL underneath; a rewrite buys nothing. You can mix Spring GraphQL APIs into a DGS application where they help.
  • Needing codegen or federation — DGS's generated types and built-in federation support are the strongest reasons to pick it for a new project.
  • Preferring code-first Kotlin — look at GraphQL Kotlin instead; it generates the schema from Kotlin code rather than requiring SDL.

docs.title: In this repository
docs.text: The dgs* modules demonstrate the DGS programming model; the spring-graphql* modules demonstrate Spring GraphQL across every transport. Both sets run the same blog domain (posts, authors, comments) against the same Postgres schema, so you can compare equivalent implementations directly — for example dgs versus spring-graphql, or dgs-subscription-ws versus spring-graphql-webmvc-ws.

docs.title: Netflix DGS
docs.text: The DGS (Domain Graph Service) framework is Netflix's GraphQL server framework for Spring Boot, open-sourced in February 2021 after years of internal use. Since DGS 9 it is built on Spring GraphQL — see the integration — so this page focuses on what DGS adds on top: its programming model and tooling.

docs.title: The programming model
docs.text:
DGS is schema-first: you write SDL under src/main/resources/schema/, then implement data fetchers as annotated Spring components. The following excerpt is from PostsDataFetcher.java in the dgs example:

@DgsComponent
public class PostsDataFetcher {
    private final PostService postService;

    @DgsQuery
    public List<Post> allPosts() {
        return this.postService.getAllPosts();
    }

    @DgsQuery
    public Post postById(@InputArgument Long postId) {
        return this.postService.getPostById(postId);
    }

    @DgsData(parentType = "Post", field = "author")
    public CompletableFuture<Author> author(DgsDataFetchingEnvironment dfe) {
        DataLoader<Long, Author> dataLoader = dfe.getDataLoader("authorsLoader");
        Post post = dfe.getSource();
        return dataLoader.load(post.getAuthorId());
    }

    @DgsMutation
    public Post createPost(@InputArgument("createPostInput") CreatePostInput input) {
        var id = this.postService.createPost(input);
        return this.postService.getPostById(id);
    }
}

The annotations map directly to the schema:

  • @DgsComponent — marks the class as a data fetcher container (a Spring stereotype).
  • @DgsQuery, @DgsMutation, @DgsSubscription — bind a method to a field on the corresponding root type, matched by method name.
  • @DgsData(parentType = "...", field = "...") — binds a method to any field on any type, for nested resolution.
  • @InputArgument — binds a GraphQL argument to a method parameter, with automatic coercion to the parameter type.

Subscriptions return a reactive Publisher; the dgs-subscription-ws example shows a @DgsSubscription method backed by a Reactor Sinks.many() stream, and dgs-subscription-sse serves the same model over SSE.

docs.title: Code generation
docs.text: The DGS codegen plugin (Gradle and Maven) generates Java or Kotlin types from the schema, so data fetchers work against generated classes instead of hand-written DTOs. The dgs-codegen example demonstrates it with Spring Data JDBC.

docs.title: Federation
docs.text: DGS ships first-class support for Apollo Federation: a DGS service can act as a federated subgraph, and the framework handles entity resolution and the federation schema additions. This is one of the features DGS adds beyond Spring GraphQL.

docs.title: Testing
docs.text: The dgs-starter-test dependency provides DgsQueryExecutor, which executes documents against the application context without an HTTP round trip, and @DgsTest slices for focused query tests. Since the Spring GraphQL integration, DgsQueryExecutor delegates to Spring GraphQL's execution service, so existing tests keep working.

docs.title: File uploads
docs.text: DGS resolves multipart uploads to Spring MultipartFile arguments — see File upload and the dgs-fileupload example.

docs.title: Versions and compatibility
docs.text:
DGS releases a platform BOM, graphql-dgs-platform-dependencies, that aligns the DGS artifacts with a Spring Boot version. The examples in this repository use DGS platform 12.1.0 on Spring Boot 4.1.2. The upstream compatibility matrix:

DGS version Spring Boot Status 11+ 4 Actively maintained. 10.x 3 Most features backported until the second half of 2026. 5.x 2 No longer maintained.

Every DGS release since 9.0 builds on Spring GraphQL, so a DGS application can also use Spring GraphQL APIs directly — see the integration.

docs.title: The DGS and Spring GraphQL integration
docs.text: Since DGS 9.0 (May 2024), the Netflix DGS framework is built on Spring GraphQL. This page explains why the two teams merged their foundations and what the integration changes for your code. It follows Netflix's own Spring GraphQL Integration document.

docs.title: Two competing frameworks
docs.text:
Netflix open-sourced DGS in 2021, and it became the most widely adopted GraphQL Java framework. Soon after, the DGS team learned of a parallel effort by the Spring team: Spring for GraphQL, then in its early stages as a low-level integration with GraphQL Java. Over the following year Spring GraphQL matured to rough feature parity with DGS.

The result was two frameworks solving the same problem. New users had to choose between them and missed out on features available only in the other; the maintainers duplicated work instead of collaborating; and the community's feedback was split across two projects.

docs.title: Why not end-of-life one of them?
docs.text: DGS is deeply embedded in the architecture of many companies, including Netflix. Forcing those users onto Spring GraphQL would be a costly migration with no real benefit. At the same time, Spring deserves an out-of-the-box GraphQL offering, just as it has for REST. Neither framework could simply disappear.

docs.title: The way forward
docs.text: The teams chose integration over competition. DGS keeps its programming model and tooling, but drops the parts that duplicated Spring GraphQL's low-level WebMVC/WebFlux integration. The integration shipped first as an opt-in spring-graphql flavor of the DGS starter, then became the default in DGS 9.0 (May 2024), which builds against Spring GraphQL 1.3, Spring Boot 3.3, and GraphQL Java 22.

docs.title: Technical implementation
docs.text:
Both frameworks were designed for modularity, which made the integration feasible. Before the integration, a request flowed through DGS's own transport integration and its DgsQueryExecutor, which called GraphQL Java directly. After the integration:

  • You write data fetchers with the DGS programming model (@DgsComponent, @DgsQuery), the Spring GraphQL programming model (@QueryMapping), or both in the same application.
  • DGS builds the GraphQLSchema from its programming model and schema files.
  • Spring GraphQL handles the transports: WebMvc, WebFlux, and RSocket.
  • Spring GraphQL's ExecutionGraphQlService executes every operation.
  • DgsQueryExecutor becomes a proxy over ExecutionGraphQlService, so existing DGS test code continues to work unchanged.

One engine, one transport layer, two programming models.

docs.title: Performance
docs.text: Netflix tested the integration on some of its largest services. The tests uncovered a few performance issues in Spring WebMVC and Spring GraphQL; the Spring team addressed them quickly, and the integrated stack now performs better than the baseline of Netflix applications running the standalone DGS framework.

docs.title: What changes for your code
docs.text:
The integration is mostly a drop-in replacement — no breaking changes in the DGS programming model itself. The areas to review when upgrading are the ones where the frameworks overlapped: configuration properties, file uploads, WebSocket subscriptions, schema inspection, and test setup. Netflix's integration document lists the notable changes and known gaps per area.

For a new application, the practical consequence is that the choice between DGS and Spring GraphQL is no longer a choice of engine — see DGS or Spring GraphQL?.

docs.title: Spring GraphQL
docs.text: Spring GraphQL is the Spring team's official GraphQL support, built on GraphQL Java. Version 1.0 arrived in May 2022, and Spring Boot 2.7 introduced spring-boot-starter-graphql. It provides the transport, execution, testing, and client infrastructure that the other frameworks in this repository either use directly (DGS) or preceded (Kickstart).

docs.title: The controller model
docs.text:
Spring GraphQL is schema-first: SDL files live under src/main/resources/graphql/ by default. Annotated controllers bind methods to schema fields, in the same style as Spring MVC. The following excerpt is from PostController.java in the spring-graphql-webmvc-http example:

@Controller
public class PostController {
    private final PostService postService;

    @QueryMapping
    public List<Post> allPosts() {
        return this.postService.getAllPosts();
    }

    @QueryMapping
    public Post postById(@Argument("postId") String id) {
        return this.postService.getPostById(id);
    }

    @MutationMapping
    public Post createPost(@Argument("createPostInput") @Valid CreatePostInput input) {
        return postService.createPost(input);
    }

    @SubscriptionMapping
    public Publisher<Comment> commentAdded() {
        return this.postService.commentAdded();
    }

    @SchemaMapping(field = "author")
    public CompletionStage<Author> authorOfPost(
            Post post, DataLoader<String, Author> authorDataLoader) {
        return authorDataLoader.load(post.getAuthorId());
    }
}

The annotations mirror Spring MVC's mapping style:

  • @QueryMapping, @MutationMapping, @SubscriptionMapping — bind a method to a root-type field, matched by method name.
  • @SchemaMapping — bind a method to a field on any type; the parent object arrives as a parameter.
  • @Argument — bind a GraphQL argument, with coercion and Bean Validation (@Valid) support.

Controller methods can return plain values, CompletionStage, or reactive types (Mono, Flux, Publisher).

docs.title: Data loading
docs.text:
Spring GraphQL wraps GraphQL Java's DataLoader mechanism in a BatchLoaderRegistry. Register loaders by name or by key/value type pair, and inject them into controller methods:

registry.forTypePair(String.class, Author.class)
        .registerBatchLoader((keys, env) ->
                Flux.fromIterable(authorService.getAuthorByIdIn(keys)));

The authorOfPost method above receives the loader as a parameter — no string lookup required. See GraphQL Java for the N+1 problem this solves.

docs.title: Transports
docs.text:
Spring GraphQL separates execution from transport, and the same application code runs on every supported transport:

Transport Operations Repository example WebMvc or WebFlux over HTTP Queries, mutations; subscriptions over SSE spring-graphql-webmvc-http, spring-graphql-webflux-http HTTP + WebSocket Queries and mutations over HTTP; subscriptions over graphql-transport-ws spring-graphql-webmvc-http-ws, spring-graphql-webflux-http-ws WebSocket only Every operation over graphql-transport-ws spring-graphql-webmvc-ws, spring-graphql-webflux-ws RSocket Every operation over RSocket spring-graphql-rsocket-kotlin-co

Configuration lives under spring.graphql.*, for example the WebSocket endpoint:

spring.graphql.websocket.path=/subscriptions

docs.title: Testing
docs.text:
Spring GraphQL ships a dedicated testing API, demonstrated in three tiers by every spring-graphql-web* module:

  • @GraphQlTest slices with a protocol-neutral GraphQlTester bound to the in-JVM execution service — fast tests with the service layer mocked.
  • HttpGraphQlTester and WebSocketGraphQlTester — the same tester API over real transports against a running application.
  • The runtime client API — HttpSyncGraphQlClient (on RestClient), HttpGraphQlClient (on WebClient), and WebSocketGraphQlClient — the code a real client writes, and the tier that proves SSE subscriptions.

docs.title: Clients
docs.text: The same GraphQlClient API used in tests is the production client: HttpSyncGraphQlClient for blocking HTTP, HttpGraphQlClient for reactive HTTP and SSE, and WebSocketGraphQlClient for WebSocket. The dgs-client example shows the DGS alternative, a typesafe client generated from the schema.

docs.title: Security and observability
docs.text: Spring GraphQL integrates with Spring Security for authentication and authorization at the transport and data-fetcher level, and with Micrometer for metrics and tracing of execution. Both are standard Spring Boot auto-configurations.

docs.title: Introduction to GraphQL
docs.text:
GraphQL is a query language for APIs and a runtime for executing those queries against your data. Facebook's mobile apps have been powered by GraphQL since 2012. The specification was open-sourced in 2015, and it is now supported by the GraphQL Foundation, hosted by the non-profit Linux Foundation since 2018.

A GraphQL server exposes a single endpoint and a strongly typed schema. The client sends a document that describes exactly the data it needs, and the server responds with JSON in the same shape. Compared with a REST API, this moves the choice of response shape from the server to the client: no over-fetching fixed payloads, and no chaining multiple endpoint calls to assemble one screen.

The specification defines three kinds of operations:

  • Query — read data.
  • Mutation — write data, executed serially in the order the document lists them.
  • Subscription — a long-lived operation that pushes a stream of results to the client as events happen.

The specification deliberately says nothing about the transport. HTTP and WebSocket are the common choices, and separate specifications cover them.

docs.title: In this section
docs.text:
Read the pages in order for a complete picture of the protocol:

  1. Specification and schema — the specification editions and the schema definition language (SDL).
  2. Requests and responses — the document, variables, and the data/errors response envelope.
  3. File upload — the multipart request specification and the Upload scalar.
  4. GraphQL over HTTP — the HTTP transport, media types, status codes, and Server-Sent Events.
  5. Subscriptions over WebSocket — the deprecated subscriptions-transport-ws protocol and its replacement, graphql-ws.

docs.title: File upload
docs.text: The GraphQL specification does not define file uploads. The interoperable standard is the GraphQL multipart request specification, which defines a multipart form structure that clients and servers from different ecosystems can share. This page explains that structure and shows how the examples in this repository receive uploads.

docs.title: The Upload scalar
docs.text:
A schema that accepts files declares a custom scalar, conventionally named Upload, and uses it in a mutation:

scalar Upload

type Mutation {
    upload(file: Upload!): Boolean
}

Uploads are mutations: they change server state, so they never run over HTTP GET.

docs.title: The multipart form structure
docs.text:
A multipart request follows RFC 7578 and orders its fields so the server can resolve the operation while the files are still uploading:

  1. operations — a JSON-encoded operations object (the usual query, variables, and operationName), with every file value replaced by null.
  2. map — a JSON-encoded map from each file's form field name to an array of object paths locating that file inside operations, for example variables.file.
  3. One field per file — the file itself, under the field name the map references.

The following request uploads a single file a.txt to the dgs-fileupload example:

curl http://localhost:8080/graphql \
  -F operations='{ "query": "mutation ($file: Upload!) { upload(file: $file) }", "variables": { "file": null } }' \
  -F map='{ "0": ["variables.file"] }' \
  -F 0=@a.txt

The specification also supports file lists (variables.files.0, variables.files.1), files nested anywhere in the variables, operation batching, and file deduplication — one file field can map to several paths.

docs.title: Receiving uploads in DGS
docs.text:
The DGS framework maps the file to a Spring MultipartFile. The following excerpt is from FileUploadMutation.java:

@DgsComponent
public class FileUploadMutation {

    @DgsMutation
    public Boolean upload(DgsDataFetchingEnvironment env) {
        var file = (MultipartFile) env.getArgument("file");
        // read file.getInputStream(), file.getOriginalFilename(), ...
        return true;
    }
}

docs.title: Receiving uploads in Spring GraphQL
docs.text:
Spring GraphQL binds the file the same way. The following excerpt is from DataFetchers.java in the spring-graphql example:

public DataFetcher<Boolean> upload() {
    return (DataFetchingEnvironment dfe) -> {
        MultipartFile file = dfe.getArgument("file");
        String content = StreamUtils.copyToString(
                file.getInputStream(), StandardCharsets.UTF_8);
        return true;
    };
}

In both frameworks the multipart parsing happens in the transport layer; the data fetcher only sees the resolved MultipartFile argument.

docs.title: GraphQL over HTTP
docs.text: The GraphQL specification deliberately does not define a transport. For years the closest thing to official guidance was the Serving over HTTP article, and leading clients and servers converged on its conventions. The GraphQL over HTTP specification formalizes those conventions for interoperability; it is a work in progress (Stage 2: Draft), but its core rules already describe what most servers do.

docs.title: POST
docs.text: A server MUST support GraphQL requests via POST with a UTF-8 JSON body and the Content-Type: application/json header. The body carries the query, variables, and operationName members described in Requests and responses. Every example in this repository accepts POST on /graphql.

docs.title: GET
docs.text: A server MAY support GET for queries. The request parameters move into the URL query string: query, variables (JSON-encoded), and operationName. GET requests MUST NOT execute mutations — the recommended response is 405 Method Not Allowed with an Allow header. GET is useful for caching read-only queries, but it is optional; do not rely on it being enabled.

docs.title: Media types and status codes
docs.text:
The specification registers two media types:

Media type Purpose application/json GraphQL JSON requests. application/graphql-response+json GraphQL JSON responses.

A client that understands the new response media type sends it in the Accept header, typically as application/graphql-response+json, application/json;q=0.9 so older servers can fall back to plain JSON.

The media type decides how errors map to HTTP status codes:

  • With application/graphql-response+json, a request-level error (invalid document, validation failure, malformed JSON) produces a 4xx or 5xx status code. A well-formed operation that executes — even with field errors — produces a 2xx status code.
  • With legacy application/json responses, most servers return 200 OK for any well-formed response and signal problems only in the errors member.

This is why a GraphQL client must always inspect the response body: a 200 status does not mean every field succeeded.

docs.title: Subscriptions over HTTP: Server-Sent Events
docs.text:
Subscriptions need a channel that stays open. Over plain HTTP, the examples in this repository use Server-Sent Events (SSE): the client POSTs the subscription document with Accept: text/event-stream, and the server keeps the response open and writes one data: event per result. The graphql-sse library implements this pattern on the client side.

The -http modules — for example spring-graphql-webmvc-http and dgs-subscription-sse — serve queries, mutations, and SSE subscriptions on the same /graphql endpoint. For a bidirectional channel that also carries queries and mutations, see Subscriptions over WebSocket.

docs.title: GraphiQL
docs.text: GraphiQL is an in-browser IDE for exploring a GraphQL endpoint: it reads the schema through introspection and provides completion, documentation, and a query runner. Spring GraphQL serves it when spring.graphql.graphiql.enabled=true; in this repository the two -http modules enable it, and the other spring-graphql-web* modules disable it.

docs.title: Requests and responses
docs.text: This page shows the shape of a GraphQL request and response. The examples run against the schema in Specification and schema, which the dgs and spring-graphql examples expose at http://localhost:8080/graphql.

docs.title: The request
docs.text:
A GraphQL request carries three members:

  • query — the document: one or more operations, each a query, mutation, or subscription.
  • variables — a JSON object of values for the variables the document declares. Optional.
  • operationName — which operation to run when the document contains more than one. Optional.

Over HTTP, the client POSTs this as a JSON body. The following request reads every post with its title and author name:

curl http://localhost:8080/graphql \
  -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
  -d '{"query": "{ allPosts { id title author { name } } }"}'

docs.title: Variables
docs.text:
Never build a document by concatenating user input into the query string. Declare variables instead, and let the server coerce and validate them:

curl http://localhost:8080/graphql \
  -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
  -d '{
    "query": "query PostById($postId: ID!) { postById(postId: $postId) { title content } }",
    "variables": { "postId": "1" },
    "operationName": "PostById"
  }'

The document declares $postId: ID!; the variables object supplies the value. The server validates the document against the schema before any data fetcher runs.

docs.title: Mutations
docs.text:
A mutation uses the same envelope. The following request creates a post with the CreatePostInput input type:

curl http://localhost:8080/graphql \
  -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
  -d '{
    "query": "mutation CreatePost($input: CreatePostInput!) { createPost(createPostInput: $input) { id title } }",
    "variables": { "input": { "title": "Hello GraphQL", "content": "First post" } }
  }'

docs.title: The response
docs.text:
A GraphQL response is a JSON object with up to three members:

  • data — the result, in the same shape as the operation's selection set.
  • errors — a list of errors raised while validating or executing the operation. Present only when something went wrong.
  • extensions — an optional map for server-specific additions, such as tracing data.

A successful response to the allPosts query looks like this:

{
  "data": {
    "allPosts": [
      { "id": "1", "title": "Hello GraphQL", "author": { "name": "Hantsy" } }
    ]
  }
}

docs.title: Partial data and field errors
docs.text:
GraphQL distinguishes request errors from field errors. A request error — a syntax error, a validation failure, an unknown operation — rejects the whole operation, and the response has errors and no data. A field error — a data fetcher that throws — nulls out only that field, and the rest of the response still returns:

{
  "data": {
    "postById": {
      "title": "Hello GraphQL",
      "author": null
    }
  },
  "errors": [
    {
      "message": "Failed to load author",
      "locations": [{ "line": 1, "column": 40 }],
      "path": ["postById", "author"]
    }
  ]
}

Each error carries a message, the locations in the document that caused it, and the path to the field that failed. If a non-null field (Author!) errors, the null propagates up to the nearest nullable parent — the schema's nullability rules decide how much of the response survives.

This envelope is the same over every transport. See GraphQL over HTTP for how HTTP status codes interact with it, and Subscriptions over WebSocket for how a stream of these envelopes reaches the client.

docs.title: Specification and schema
docs.text: This page explains what the GraphQL specification covers and how to read and write the schema definition language (SDL). It is for developers who are new to GraphQL; it does not cover any Java API.

docs.title: The specification
docs.text:
The GraphQL specification defines the query language, the type system, validation rules, execution semantics, and introspection. It deliberately does not define a transport — see GraphQL over HTTP and Subscriptions over WebSocket for the transport specifications.

The specification is published in dated editions:

Edition Notes June 2018 The first stable edition after the 2015 open-source release. October 2021 Adds custom scalar semantics clarifications and repeatable directives. September 2025 The latest released edition.

A draft of the next edition is also published. Every server implementation — including GraphQL Java — implements the language and execution rules from these editions.

docs.title: The schema definition language
docs.text:
A GraphQL schema is a contract written in SDL. It declares the types a server exposes and the operations clients can run. The following schema is the one used by the dgs example (comments and formatting trimmed):

type Post {
    id: ID!
    title: String!
    content: String
    comments: [Comment]
    authorId: String
    author: Author
}

type Author {
    id: ID!
    name: String!
    email: String!
    posts: [Post]
}

type Comment {
    id: ID!
    content: String!
    postId: String!
}

input CreatePostInput {
    title: String!
    content: String!
}

type Query {
    allPosts: [Post!]!
    postById(postId: ID!): Post
}

type Mutation {
    createPost(createPostInput: CreatePostInput!): Post!
}

The building blocks are:

  • Object types (type Post) — named collections of fields. Each field has a type and can take arguments, such as postById(postId: ID!).
  • Scalar types — the leaf values. The built-in scalars are Int, Float, String, Boolean, and ID. Servers can add custom scalars such as Date or Upload.
  • Input types (input CreatePostInput) — structured arguments for mutations. Only input types, scalars, and enums can be used as input.
  • Enums — a fixed set of named values, for example enum PostStatus { DRAFT PUBLISHED }.
  • Interfaces and unions — abstract types that let a field return one of several object types. A TypeResolver picks the concrete type at runtime.
  • Non-null (!) and lists ([]) — modifiers. Post! never returns null, [Post!]! is a non-null list of non-null posts, and [Post] can be null and can contain nulls.
  • Directives — annotations such as @deprecated(reason: "...") that change how the schema or a document is executed. Servers can define custom directives.

docs.title: Root operation types
docs.text:
Three root types anchor every schema:

  • Query — the entry point for reads.
  • Mutation — the entry point for writes. Top-level mutation fields execute serially, in document order; query fields can execute in parallel.
  • Subscription — the entry point for event streams. A subscription field returns a stream of results rather than a single value.

The names are conventions; the schema can rename them with a schema declaration, but most servers — and every example in this repository — use the default names.

docs.title: Introspection
docs.text:
A GraphQL schema is queryable. Clients can ask the server for its own types through the meta-fields __schema and __type, which is how tools such as GraphiQL and Apollo Client provide completion and documentation. The following query lists every type name the server exposes:

{
  __schema {
    types {
      name
    }
  }
}

Introspection is part of the specification, so it works against any compliant server, including all examples in this repository.

docs.title: Subscriptions over WebSocket
docs.text: A subscription is a long-lived operation: the server pushes a new result every time an event happens. Plain HTTP request/response cannot carry that, so subscription clients and servers agree on a WebSocket subprotocol. Two protocols exist, and they are not compatible with each other — the client and the server must speak the same one.

docs.title: subscriptions-transport-ws (deprecated)
docs.text:
subscriptions-transport-ws was the first WebSocket transport for GraphQL subscriptions, created by Apollo in 2016. It was largely unmaintained after 2018, and its repository now states that the project is no longer maintained and that users should migrate to graphql-ws.

The protocol uses the WebSocket subprotocol graphql-ws. Its messages, prefixed GQL_ in the reference implementation, are:

Message Direction Purpose connection_init client → server Initialize the connection, optionally with a payload (for example, auth tokens). connection_ack server → client Acknowledge the connection. connection_keep_alive server → client Periodic heartbeat (ka) after the ack. start client → server Start an operation with an id and a GraphQL payload. data server → client One execution result for a started operation. error server → client Operation failed before execution (for example, validation errors). complete server → client The operation's stream is finished. stop client → server Stop a running operation. connection_terminate client → server Close the connection.

Only subscriptions were intended to run over this protocol; queries and mutations stayed on HTTP.

docs.title: graphql-ws
docs.text:
graphql-ws is the actively maintained replacement. Its protocol, the GraphQL over WebSocket Protocol, uses the subprotocol graphql-transport-ws. The message flow is similar, but the protocol fixes the gaps of its predecessor:

Message Direction Purpose ConnectionInit client → server Initialize the connection. More than one init closes the socket (4429). ConnectionAck server → client Acknowledge; operations are allowed only after the ack (otherwise 4401). Subscribe client → server Start any operation — query, mutation, or subscription — under a unique id. A duplicate id closes the socket (4409). Next server → client One execution result from the operation's stream. Error server → client Execution errors for the operation; the stream is finished. Complete either The stream is finished; the client can also send it to unsubscribe. Ping / Pong either Bidirectional heartbeat, sent at any time; a Pong may also be unsolicited.

The differences that matter in practice:

  • Any operation over the socket. Queries and mutations can share the subscription connection instead of opening separate HTTP requests.
  • Real keep-alive. Both sides can ping; the old protocol only had a server-side keep-alive.
  • Defined failure semantics. Close codes such as 4401 Unauthorized, 4409 Subscriber already exists, and 4429 Too many initialisation requests replace ad-hoc behavior.

Because the protocols are distinct, migrating means upgrading the client and the server together — a graphql-ws client cannot talk to a subscriptions-transport-ws server.

docs.title: In this repository
docs.text:
The WebSocket examples all speak graphql-transport-ws:

  • dgs-subscription-ws — DGS subscriptions. A @DgsSubscription method returns a reactive Publisher; the following excerpt is from its DataFetchers.kt:
@DgsSubscription
fun messageSent(): Publisher<TextMessage> = sink.asFlux()
  • spring-graphql-webmvc-ws and spring-graphql-webflux-ws — Spring GraphQL with every operation type over WebSocket. The endpoint is configured with a property, as in spring-graphql-webmvc-http-ws:
spring.graphql.websocket.path=/subscriptions
  • The dgs-subscription-ui* Angular clients consume these streams with Apollo Client and the graphql-ws library.

If you do not need a bidirectional channel, Server-Sent Events are a simpler alternative — see GraphQL over HTTP.

docs.title: GraphQL Java
docs.text:
GraphQL Java is the JVM implementation of the GraphQL specification, started in 2015. It is an execution engine, not a server framework: it parses schemas, validates documents, and executes operations, but it knows nothing about HTTP, WebSocket, or Spring. Every framework in this repository — Spring GraphQL, Netflix DGS, and the legacy Kickstart and SPQR examples — embeds it and delegates execution to it.

This page tours the core concepts. The code excerpts come from the legacy/graphql-java example, which wires the engine by hand; the framework examples do the same wiring for you.

docs.title: Build the schema
docs.text:
Execution starts with a GraphQLSchema. The schema-first path parses SDL into a TypeDefinitionRegistry, then combines it with a RuntimeWiring to produce an executable schema:

TypeDefinitionRegistry typeRegistry =
        new SchemaParser().parse(new ClassPathResource("/schema/schema.graphql").getFile());

GraphQLSchema graphQLSchema =
        new SchemaGenerator().makeExecutableSchema(typeRegistry, runtimeWiring);

RuntimeWiring is where behavior attaches to the type system: data fetchers, custom scalars, directives, and type resolvers for interfaces and unions. The legacy example builds it with a code registry that maps fields to fetchers:

RuntimeWiring.newRuntimeWiring()
        .codeRegistry(codeRegistry)
        .scalar(Scalars.localDateTimeType())
        .scalar(Scalars.uuidType())
        .directive("uppercase", new UpperCaseDirectiveWiring())
        .build();

A code-first path also exists — building GraphQLSchema programmatically with builders instead of SDL — but every example in this repository is schema-first.

docs.title: Fetch data
docs.text:
A DataFetcher<T> resolves one field. It receives a DataFetchingEnvironment with the field arguments, the parent object (getSource()), the execution context, and the data loader registry:

public DataFetcher<Post> postById() {
    return (DataFetchingEnvironment dfe) -> {
        String postId = dfe.getArgument("postId");
        return postService.getPostById(postId);
    };
}

Fields without an explicit fetcher fall back to PropertyDataFetcher, which reads a matching property from the parent object — this is why a Post record with a title accessor needs no wiring for its title field.

A fetcher can return a plain value, a CompletionStage for asynchronous work, or a reactive Publisher for subscription fields.

docs.title: Execute operations
docs.text:
The GraphQL object is the engine entry point. Build it once from the schema, then execute an ExecutionInput per request:

GraphQL graphQL = GraphQL.newGraphQL(graphQLSchema).build();

ExecutionInput input = ExecutionInput.newExecutionInput()
        .query("{ allPosts { id title } }")
        .build();

ExecutionResult result = graphQL.execute(input);
Map<String, Object> data = result.getData();
List<GraphQLError> errors = result.getErrors();

executeAsync returns a CompletableFuture<ExecutionResult> instead. The ExecutionResult maps directly to the response envelope described in Requests and responses.

The engine picks an execution strategy per operation type: query fields resolve in parallel, mutation fields resolve serially in document order, and subscription fields resolve to a stream that the transport layer forwards to the client.

docs.title: Batch with DataLoader
docs.text:
Naive field resolution produces the N+1 problem: loading ten posts and then each post's comments runs eleven queries. The java-dataloader library — a separate project under the GraphQL Java organization — batches and caches loads per request. The repository's DataLoaders notes show the effect on SQL. Before, one query per post:

SELECT * FROM comments WHERE post_id = ?
SELECT * FROM comments WHERE post_id = ?
SELECT * FROM comments WHERE post_id = ?

After, one batched query:

SELECT * FROM comments WHERE post_id in (?, ?, ?, ?)

A fetcher asks the environment for a registered loader and loads a key; the loader collects keys during the execution tick and dispatches them as one batch:

DataLoader<String, Author> dataLoader = dfe.getDataLoader("authorsLoader");
return dataLoader.load(post.getAuthorId());

Loaders are registered in a DataLoaderRegistry keyed by name. Spring GraphQL and DGS both build on this same mechanism — see Spring GraphQL for its BatchLoaderRegistry convenience.

docs.title: Extend execution
docs.text:
The engine exposes several extension points, all demonstrated in the repository:

  • Instrumentation — hooks around parsing, validation, and execution for metrics and tracing. GraphQL Java 22 reworked this API; older examples use the pre-22 form.
  • Error handling — a DataFetcherExceptionHandler decides how a fetcher exception becomes a GraphQLError (see CustomDataFetchingExceptionHandler in the legacy example).
  • Custom scalars — a Coercing implementation parses input and serializes output for scalars such as LocalDateTime and UUID (see Scalars.java).
  • Directives — a SchemaDirectiveWiring wraps field fetchers to implement custom directives (see UpperCaseDirectiveWiring).

docs.title: Where to go next
docs.text: The raw wiring above is what the frameworks automate. Read Integration history for how the JVM ecosystem arrived at Spring GraphQL and DGS, then see Netflix DGS and Spring GraphQL for the two programming models.

docs.title: Integration history
docs.text: GraphQL on the JVM has gone through several generations of integration libraries. This page traces that history — it explains why this repository keeps a frozen legacy/ folder, and why the two actively developed frameworks today, Spring GraphQL and Netflix DGS, share the same engine. The framework links come from the README.

docs.title: 2015: GraphQL Java
docs.text: Facebook open-sourced the GraphQL specification in 2015, and GraphQL Java started the same year as the JVM implementation. It provided schema parsing, validation, and execution — but no way to serve requests. Integrating it into an application meant writing your own endpoint.

docs.title: 2016: graphql-java-servlet
docs.text: graphql-java-servlet (2016) filled the gap with a servlet endpoint: it accepted GraphQL requests over HTTP and handed them to a GraphQL instance. It also carried an early WebSocket subscription implementation from the subscriptions-transport-ws era (see Subscriptions over WebSocket).

docs.title: The Kickstart era
docs.text:
The GraphQL Java Kickstart project built the most popular Spring Boot integration of that period on two pieces:

  • GraphQL Java Tools — a schema-first tool inspired by JavaScript's graphql-tools: you write SDL and implement resolver interfaces, and the library wires them into a RuntimeWiring.
  • GraphQL Spring Boot Starters — auto-configuration for the servlet, GraphiQL, and subscriptions.

This repository's legacy/graphql-java-kickstart* examples use that stack. The starters are now archived; the repository's notice reads:

Since Spring now officially supports GraphQL we have decided to archive this project. We encourage you to start using Spring for GraphQL instead.

docs.title: The code-first alternative: SPQR
docs.text: GraphQL SPQR (Schema Publisher & Query Resolver, pronounced "speaker") took the opposite approach: annotate plain Java methods and let the library generate the schema from the code. Development is no longer active; the legacy/graphql-spqr example is frozen.

docs.title: 2021: Netflix DGS
docs.text: Netflix open-sourced the DGS (Domain Graph Service) framework in February 2021, after years of internal use. It offered an annotation-based Spring Boot programming model, schema code generation, federation support, and a query-test framework. See the announcement posts: Open Sourcing the Netflix Domain Graph Service Framework and InfoQ's coverage of the release and Netflix's GraphQL microservices architecture.

docs.title: 2021–2022: Spring GraphQL
docs.text: Soon after DGS appeared, the Spring team started a parallel effort: Spring GraphQL, built directly on GraphQL Java. Version 1.0 arrived in May 2022, and Spring Boot 2.7 shipped spring-boot-starter-graphql — GraphQL became an official part of the Spring portfolio, with first-class WebMvc, WebFlux, WebSocket, and RSocket transports and the GraphQlTester testing API.

docs.title: 2023–2024: convergence
docs.text: Two frameworks solving the same problem split the community. Instead of end-of-lifing either one, the teams integrated them: DGS adopted Spring GraphQL as its execution foundation, first as an opt-in starter flavor, then by default in DGS 9.0 (May 2024, on Spring GraphQL 1.3). The DGS and Spring GraphQL integration page tells that story in detail.

docs.title: The ecosystem today
docs.text:
Project Approach Status GraphQL Java Execution engine Active; the foundation of everything below. Spring GraphQL Official Spring integration, schema-first controllers Active; the Spring baseline. Netflix DGS Annotation model, codegen, federation, on Spring GraphQL Active. GraphQL Kotlin Code-first Kotlin, coroutines (ExpediaGroup) Active. GraphQL Java Kickstart Schema-first tools + Spring Boot starters Starters archived; use Spring GraphQL. GraphQL SPQR Code-first schema generation Inactive.

Other JVM frameworks integrate GraphQL Java outside Spring as well — see GraphQL with Quarkus and GraphQL with Vert.x.

The legacy/ folder in this repository preserves the discontinued stacks (Kickstart, SPQR, vanilla GraphQL Java) on the Spring Boot and Java versions they were last verified with, excluded from dependency updates. The active modules track current Spring Boot and either Spring GraphQL or DGS.
